Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

strengths: QuEST presents a useful empirical contribution to diffusion-model compression. Selectively finetuning temporal and attention-related layers with local and global supervision is practical, requires no original training images or additional adapters, and reportedly updates less than 7% of LDM-4 parameters.

The evaluation covers unconditional, class-conditional, and text-to-image generation, with 50,000-image evaluations for LDMs. On Bedrooms W4A8, FID improves from 5.37 for Q-Diffusion and 3.68 for TFMQ-DM to 3.26, approaching the full-precision result of 2.95. W4A4 also substantially improves over the reported EfficientDM baseline.

The component ablations provide meaningful support: Table 6 improves FID from 6.95 to 4.41 with temporal alignment and then to 3.26 with critical-module alignment. Table 7 supports combining local and global supervision. Activation-distribution plots and token-corruption experiments provide complementary motivation.

The high-level method is clearly presented, relevant datasets and prior methods are cited, and a code-release link is supplied. The supplement adds comparisons and qualitative results, and appropriately identifies possible effects of quantization on watermarking and safety mechanisms.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is not sound as written. For the stated MSE on final outputs, the Taylor expansion is exactly quadratic; large perturbations alone do not invalidate it. Moreover, Eq. (11) contains quadratic terms in the small increment epsilon, whereas Eq. (10) substitutes cumulative output residuals without justification. The asserted bound permitting omission of the second-order term is not established. These issues weaken the theoretical contribution, although the paper explicitly disclaims a guarantee and the empirical method can stand independently.

Efficiency accounting needs clarification. Table 6 reports 15.25 GPU hours and FID 3.26 for QuEST at W4A8, while Table 8 reports 0.45 hours and FID 3.82 for LDM-4 at the same precision. Different schedules or excluded initialization costs could explain this, but the manuscript does not reconcile them. Consistent accounting of calibration generation, initialization, and finetuning is necessary to assess the central efficiency claim. Actual low-bit inference latency is also unmeasured.

The closest-baseline comparisons need stronger documentation. EfficientDM reportedly fails at W8A8 on both LSUN datasets, yet succeeds at W4A4; its Bedrooms W4A8 FID is also worse than W4A4. These outcomes warrant explanation and validation. Exact quantization exceptions, initialization choices, batch sizes, and per-stage training schedules are insufficiently specified to reproduce and assess the comparisons.

The distinctive module selection and progressive schedule are only partially isolated. Table 6 establishes benefits from adding components, but does not compare against similarly sized alternative trainable subsets or joint training under a matched budget. Figure 3 identifies feedforward sensitivity, while the method selects the broader attention-related subset. Stronger controls would establish why this particular selection and ordering matter beyond additional finetuning.

Evidence for quality preservation is weaker at W4A4, particularly for text-to-image generation. ImageNet IS falls from 364.73 to 202.45 despite improved FID, and Stable Diffusion is evaluated quantitatively only through CLIP Score, which cannot establish perceptual fidelity. The visible W4A4 degradation and narrow text-to-image baseline coverage limit broad quality claims, while leaving the reported improvements over existing low-bit baselines meaningful.
